title: Revisiting the Grain and Valence Effect of Oxide-Derived Copper on Electrocatalytic CO2 Reduction Using Single Crystal Cu(111) Foils
abstract: Oxide-derived Cu (OD-Cu) has been viewed as a highly active form for catalyzing the multielectron transfer of electrochemical CO2 reduction, but the underlying catalytic mechanism is still controversial. In the current study, the crystalline and valency factors that influence the CO2R activities of OD-Cu are revisited by employing single crystal Cu(111) foils that exclude convolutions from initial morphological and crystallographic heterogeneity. We observe that the overall CO2R performance, especially the C2H4 selectivity, correlates well with the initial oxidation level of the Cu(111) foil, of which the surface oxide layer is reduced into small fragments comprising rich grain boundaries and diversely orientated facets. Nonetheless, we find that the polycrystallinity and grain boundaries of OD-Cu, in this circumstance, are not the major causes of the observed activity enhancement. Instead, a transition state between the initial oxide and the finally reduced copper phases, as well as its longevity, dictates the catalytic property of OD-Cu in electrochemical CO2 reduction. Consequently, this work furnishes further evidence and in-depth understanding to help clarify the catalytic mechanism of OD-Cu in CO2R. R CO2 utilization, by simultaneously reducing the green-house gas and producing value-added chemical fuels and feedstocks, holds great promise to meet the demand of attaining a carbon-neutral economy in the nearest future. Of particular interest, electrocatalytic CO2 reduction (CO2R) employing green and renewable energy input has gained tremendous attention due to the readily available infrastructure and well-established electrolytic industry. In order to maximize the economic merits of this technique, it is key to produce high value-added products with high yield and selectivity while minimizing the energy input, which in turn requires highly efficient electrocatalysts. To date, copper has still been perceived as the only single metal capable of catalyzing CO2 conversion into a variety of >2e − hydrocarbons and oxygenates, by virtue of its modest binding to many of the key CO2R intermediates including *CO, *CHO, *OCCO, etc. On the other hand, the linear scaling relationship among the binding strengths of these various intermediates would unavoidably lead to poor product selectivity, and thus the conflict between diversity and specificity, both are in fact desired, has to be reconciled by meticulous catalyst design guided by mechanistic understanding. Yet, there has been no explicit consensus on the catalytic mechanism of Cu toward >2e− reduction products. The controversy mainly lies in the ever-changing crystallographic and oxidation states of Cu-based catalysts under the highly reductive CO2R conditions. 13−16 This is particularly the case for oxide-derived copper (OD-Cu), which typically manifests much improved CO2R performance when compared to pristine Cu. While some studies suggest that the OD-Cu is fully reduced at the CO2R condition and relate the high C2+ selectivity to defect-rich Cu states such as high-index facets, undercoordinated atoms, and intertwining grain boundaries, others attribute it to the persistence of a positive Cu valence balanced by subsurface oxygen, or a metastable state liable to oxidation. For instance, in the study by Lei et al., oxidized Cu was pretreated to fully reduce oxides/hydroxides to Cu and showed even better C2+ selectivity compared to their untreated counterparts. Focused ion beam (FIB) in conjunction with transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) analyses revealed the fragmentation of oxide/ hydroxide crystals into nanosized irregular Cu grains under the applied negative potentials, exposing rich grain boundaries and high-index facets accounting for the enhanced C2+ selectivity. Resourceful CO2 utilization, by simultaneously reducingthe green-house gas and producing value-added chemical fuels and feedstocks, holds great promise to meet the demand of attaining a carbon-neutral economy in the nearest future.1,2 Of particular interest, electrocatalytic CO2 reduction (CO2R) employing green and renewable energy input has gained tremendous attention due to the readily available infrastructure and well-established electrolytic industry.3,4 In order to maximize the economic merits of this technique, it is key to produce high value-added products with high yield and selectivity while minimizing the energy input, which in turn requires highly efficient electrocatalysts.5,6 To date, copper has still been perceived as the only single metal capable of catalyzing CO2 conversion into a variety of >2e
− hydrocarbons and oxygenates, by virtue of its modest binding to many of the key CO2R intermediates including *CO, *CHO, *OCCO, etc.7,8 On the other hand, the linear scaling relationship among the binding strengths of these various intermediates would unavoidably lead to poor product selectivity,9,10 and thus the conflict between diversity and specificity, both are in fact desired, has to be reconciled by meticulous catalyst design guided by mechanistic understanding. Yet, there has been no explicit consensus on the catalytic mechanism of Cu toward >2e− reduction products.11,12 The controversy mainly lies in the ever-changing crystallographic and oxidation states of Cu-based catalysts under the highly reductive CO2R conditions.
13−16 This is particularly the case for oxide-derived copper (OD-Cu), which typically manifests
much improved CO2R performance when compared to pristine Cu.17,18 While some studies suggest that the OD-Cu is fully reduced at the CO2R condition and relate the high C2+ selectivity to defect-rich Cu states such as high-index facets,19 undercoordinated atoms,20,21 and intertwining grain boundaries,22−24 others attribute it to the persistence of a positive Cuδ+ valence balanced by subsurface oxygen,25−28 or a metastable state liable to oxidation.29,30 For instance, in the study by Lei et al.,19 oxidized Cu was pretreated to fully reduce oxides/hydroxides to Cu0 and showed even better C2+ selectivity compared to their untreated counterparts. Focused ion beam (FIB) in conjunction with transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) analyses revealed the fragmentation of oxide/ hydroxide crystals into nanosized irregular Cu grains under the applied negative potentials, exposing rich grain boundaries and high-index facets accounting for the enhanced C2+ selectivity. Similarly, Jung et al. also observed the electrochemical fragmentation of Cu2O nanoparticles into compactly stacked smaller particles, leading to improved ethylene

While operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) showed exclusively the Cu0 state of metallic copper under CO2R conditions, the reduced small Cu entities were found more liable to oxidation when compared to larger particles.23 Using a battery cycling method, Jiang et al. fabricated cubic Cu2O surface and reduced it in situ to polycrystalline Cu nanocubes exposing Cu(100) facets with no oxygen detected by EELS, achieving a 6-fold improvement in C2+ to C1 product ratio.
31 Additionally, more studies have shown facet-specific CO2R performance of OD-Cu derived from hydroxides and oxides.32,33
In a different venue, several other studies underlined the key role of the positive Cu state and subsurface oxygen in affording high C2+ selectivity.
25,34−37 Through oxygen plasma treatment, Mistry et al. fabricated a porous oxide layer on polycrystalline Cu foils and achieved greatly enhanced ethylene production at low overpotentials. It was found that the Cu+ state is persistent through the CO2R process and serves as the active species for reducing CO2 to ethylene, whereas the surface roughness plays a more trivial role.36 It is worth noting that in their
experiments the monitoring of Cu valence was only carried out for 1 h at a modest negative bias of −0.91 V versus RHE. In another study, Eilert et al. investigated the valence structure of OD-Cu using in situ ambient pressure X-ray photoelectron microscopy and quasi in situ electron energy-loss spectroscopy and observed, despite the lack of copper oxides, a substantial amount of subsurface oxygen that contributes to the enhanced ethylene/methane ratio.25 Through quantum mechanics calculations, Xiao et al. constructed a theoretical model where Cu metal is embedded in the oxidized matrix and found that the CO2R activity is greatly enhanced at the borders of oxidized and metallic surface regions.38 The electrostatic tension between Cu+ and Cu0 surface sites creates a synergy for improving the kinetics and thermodynamics of both CO2 activation and CO dimerization. In one of our early investigations, we have also shown that the positive state of Cuδ+ (0 < δ < 1) induced by multimetallic alloying can be preserved through the CO2R process and is beneficial for C−C coupling.39
https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpclett.1c00588 J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 2021, 12, 3941−3950
3942
Despite the tremendous efforts, as of today the controversy still carries on. Part of the reason is due to the fact that many of the previous studies are based on the oxidation−reduction of polycrystalline Cu substrates/particles, which already contain numerous structural motifs such as grain boundaries, highindex facets, stepped terraces, corrugated surface, and so on.19,35,40 Since the complexity of the base material might convolute the later observations, the contributions of these structural features to the CO2R performance are mingled together so that a clear mechanistic understanding becomes very difficult. As such, a more simplified Cu structure with well-defined surface configuration should better serve the purpose. In the current study, we started from single crystal Cu(111) foils with minimal morphologic and crystallographic heterogeneities and then oxidized them to various degrees for deriving OD-Cu of different crystalline and valence states. Their capabilities in catalyzing CO2R are carefully examined to establish the structure−performance relation, of which the mechanistic understanding is further furnished by comprehensive postelectrolytic and operando characterizations. We found that for OD-Cu both the polycrystallinity and grain boundaries are not the main causes of the observed activity enhancement. Instead, a transition state between the initial oxide phase and the ultimately reduced copper, and its longevity, dictates the catalytic property of OD-Cu in electrochemical CO2R, in agreement with the aforementioned synergic Cu+/Cu0 model.38
Synthesis and Characterization of Single Crystal Cu(111) Foils. Single crystalline Cu(111) foils (hereafter abbreviated as Cu(111)) were fabricated by annealing polycrystalline copper (abbreviated as p-Cu) at high temperature in a mixed Ar/H2 gas flow, as detailed in the Experimental Section in Supporting Information. The obtained Cu(111) foil shows a uniform and monotonous color after surface oxidation at 200 °C in air (Figure S1), affirming the single crystallinity of the Cu foil with monofacet exposure.41,42 XRD taken on the Cu(111) foil displays only one family of lattice planes belonging to {111} (Figure 1a), whereas that of the p-Cu presents multiple peaks, including the low-index facets of (111), (100), (110) and the high-index facets such as (331) and (311), etc. (Figure 1g). Both SEM and high-resolution AFM images in Figure 1b and Figure 1c, respectively, show a flat surface morphology of Cu(111) lack of grain boundaries, exhibiting slip lines of ∼60° in cross angles that are typically seen for metal (111) surfaces.43 In comparison, p-Cu exhibits a much rougher surface composed of numerous grooves originating from the manufacturing process (Figure 1h,i), indicative of large crystalline and morphological heterogeneity. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was further employed to verify the crystalline unity and heterogeneity for the Cu(111) and p-Cu foils, respectively.42,43 As shown in Figure 1d, the inverse pole figure (IPF) color map in normal direction displays a uniform blue color, attesting to the single crystalline (111) facet exposure and homogeneous in-plane crystalline orientation, which is further confirmed by the even distribution of projection points in the (111) pole figure (Figure 1e). The kernel average misorientation (KAM) map on Cu(111) displays a small angular variation less than 1°, further corroborating the high uniformity of surface facet orientation (Figure 1f). On the contrary, EBSD characterizations on the p-Cu foil are drastically different. Whereas the IPF map reveals a heterogeneous arrangement of exposed facets and grain boundaries (Figure 1j), the corresponding pole
figure in Figure 1k exhibits no regular distribution pattern of projection points. The KAM map displays a larger misorientation of ∼3° (Figure 1l), further affirming its polycrystalline nature. Collectively, the EBSD characterizations above strongly attest to the successful transformation from the original polycrystalline Cu foil into a single-crystalline entity of Cu(111) upon annealing. CO2R on Pristine and Slightly Oxidized Polycrystalline and Single-Crystal Cu Foils. First of all, electrochemical CO2R tests were carried out in H-cell (Figure S2) to assess the pristine pCu and Cu(111) foils with respect to their intrinsic catalytic behavior. In order to minimize surface oxidation, the Cu(111) foils were tested immediately upon being taken out from the Ar/H2 filled CVD tube, while the p-Cu samples were reduced in H2 at 350 °C for 2 h before testing. At this annealing condition, p-Cu exhibited the same surface roughness and polycrystallinity except that the intensities of {100} peaks are comparatively intensified (Figure S3). In both cases, H2 composed the majority of the reduction products together with only a small fraction of CO (Figure S4). Specifically, on pCu, the highest Faradaic efficiency (FE) of CO was 9.2 ± 0.9% at −1.2 VRHE and the largest CO partial current density was only 0.11 ± 0.03 mA cm−2 at −1.3 VRHE. On Cu(111), the highest CO FE was 4.7 ± 0.6% observed at −1.2 VRHE, while the CO partial current density increased with the increasing bias but still only attained 0.1 mA cm−2 at −1.8 VRHE. In the current study, we did not analyze the liquid products due to the facts that the majority of reduction products are gases and the overall low Faradaic current of the tests would require a long time to collect any meaningful amount for accurate analyses. Nonetheless, the observations made here suggest that despite the possession of grain boundaries and high-index facets, the thermally annealed p-Cu manifests very limited improvement in catalyzing CO2R when compared to the single crystal Cu(111). Of note, the unusually low FEs and current densities of CO production observed here might be attributed to a few material and instrumental facts, including the following: (1) the reconstructed surface obtained by thermally annealing in H2 is thermodynamically more pristine, with lack of adequate active motifs;22 (2) the flat Cu foils with minimal surface area and porosity disfavor the triphasic CO2R reaction involving gas reactant, as previous studies have shown the increase in local roughness and porosity helps enrich CO2 concentration and increase local pH in the Helmholtz layer, thus promoting the CO2 conversion;
44,45 (3) compared to the gas diffusion electrode (GDE) loaded with nanocrystalline Cu catalysts, the intrinsically lower CO2 coverage on the copper foil electrode in the H-cell significantly dampens the kinetics of CO2R. Thus, the experimental setup engaging Cu foil in H-cell is better suited for mechanistic understanding rather than performance benchmarking. Interestingly, after the exposure to ambient air for just 1 day, both the p-Cu and Cu(111) foils showed notably improved CO2R performance. Although CO and H2 were still the only detected gaseous reduction products, both the FE and partial current density of CO are much larger. As shown in Figure S5, on p-Cu-1d (abbreviation for the polycrystalline Cu exposed in air for 1 day) the CO FE increased to 24.8 ± 6.9% at −1.4 VRHE, concomitant with a maximal partial current density of 0.4 ± 0.1% mA cm−2. Similar to the scenario of the pristine Cu(111), the CO partial current density of Cu(111)-1d increased with increasing applied negative bias, reaching 0.4 ± 0.2% mA cm−2 at −1.8 VRHE. Meanwhile, the maximal CO FE
https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpclett.1c00588 J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 2021, 12, 3941−3950
3943
was 15.2 ± 5.5% observed at −1.2 VRHE. The improved CO2R performance on both p-Cu-1d and Cu(111)-1d can be certainly attributed to their slightly oxidized surfaces, since no other modifications to the samples were made. As shown in Figure S6a,b, despite no signals of copper oxides were detectable from XRD taken on the Cu(111)-1d sample, two weak satellite peaks can be visualized from the XPS Cu 2p spectrum, indicating the existence of Cu+ species.33 As the Cu 2p binding energies between Cu0 and Cu+ differ by only 0.1 eV, it would be almost impossible to decouple them through
XPS peak deconvolution.46,47 Thus, we sought Auger electron spectroscopy (AES) on the Cu LMM signal,23 which clearly shows a Cu+ at 569.9 eV and a Cu0 at 568.0 eV (Figure S6c). CO2R on Single Crystal Cu(111) Foils with Dif ferent Oxidation Degree. In comparing the above pristine and airoxidized copper foils, we can see that even a slight surface oxidation might influence the yield and selectivity of the CO2R products. To further exclusively interrogate the effect of surface oxidation and meanwhile minimize perturbations from other factors such as the morphological and crystallographic
https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpclett.1c00588 J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 2021, 12, 3941−3950
3944
heterogeneity, we deliberately oxidized the Cu(111) surface to various degrees by annealing the samples in air at 250 °C for 5 min (referred to as Cu(111)-LO for low oxidation), 250 °C for 30 min (Cu(111)-MO for medium oxidation), and 350 °C for 60 min (Cu(111)-HO for high degree of oxidation). Parts a−c of Figure 2 show SEM images of the Cu(111)-LO, Cu(111)MO, and Cu(111)-HO surfaces, respectively. It is obvious that an oxide layer composed of fine particles was formed on the surface of all three samples and the granule size increased with the increasing oxidation level. Previous studies suggested that the oxidation layer on Cu was typically composed of an outmost CuO layer and a subsurface Cu2O layer. 48,49 However, XRD patterns shown in Figure 2d and Figure S7 only reveal peaks of Cu2O and Cu for all three samples, of which the peak intensity of Cu2O (111) at 36.7° (Cu2O: 00- 001-1142) increases with the increasing oxidation level. The lack of CuO signals in the XRD spectra is due to the thin thickness of CuO on top of Cu2O,
48 as well as the surface insensitivity of the bulk XRD technique. Raman spectra were hence taken to further dissect the surface copper oxides. As shown in Figure 2e, both signals of CuO and Cu2O can be identified from all spectra of Cu(111)LO, Cu(111)-MO, and Cu(111)-HO, with peaks at 146 and 217 cm−1 corresponding to Cu2O and with those at 298, 345, 632 cm−1 corresponding to CuO.50,51 Obviously, at lower temperature and shorter oxidation time, Cu2O overwhelms CuO in terms of peak intensity, whereas at higher oxidation level both these two components show prominent Raman peaks as in the case of Cu(111)-HO. The enriched CuO content at the outermost surface and its increase with increasing oxidation were further confirmed by XPS (Figure 2f). The high-resolution Cu 2p3/2 spectra can be deconvoluted into two subpeaks at the binding energies of 933.1 and 931.8 eV, respectively, corresponding to the Cu2+ and Cu+/Cu0 species.52,53 Quantitatively, the ratio of Cu2+:(Cu+/Cu0) on the surface of Cu(111)-LO, Cu(111)-MO, and Cu(111)-HO increased from 90%, 93.6% to 94.7%, respectively. Taken together from the above microscopic and spectroscopic analyses, we can now conclude that with the increase in oxidation level, larger CuOx granules are formed on the Cu(111) surface comprising an outmost CuO layer and a subsurface Cu2O phase. Next, the catalytic CO2R performance of Cu(111)-LO, Cu(111)-MO, and Cu(111)-HO was investigated by comparing the FE, partial current density, and yield stability of various reduction products. For Cu(111)-LO, products of CO, CH4, and C2H4 can be detected from the gaseous elution at −1.3 VRHE, and prior to that CO and H2 were the major reduction products (Figure 3a, Figure S8). While the FE of C2H4 reached its maximum at −1.6 VRHE, that of CH4 rose continuously with the decreasing potential. The largest partial current density of CO and C2H4 was 0.6 ± 0.1 mA cm −2 and 0.7 ± 0.1 mA cm−2 at −1.8 VRHE, while that of CH4 was 1.0 ± 0.1 mA cm−2 at −1.9 VRHE (Figure S9). A similar trend of FE was also observed for Cu(111)-MO, except the FEs of C2H4 were more than doubled with the highest value of 19.7 ± 1.1% observed at −1.8 VRHE (Figure 3b). While both the partial current densities of H2 and CO decreased, the yield rates of C2H4 and CH4 (e.g., 1.8 ± 0.5 and 2.2 ± 0.1 mA cm−2 at −1.9 VRHE for CH4 and C2H4, respectively) are drastically promoted when compared to those of Cu(111)-LO (Figure S10 vs Figure S9). For Cu(111)-HO, CO, and C2H4 constitute the major reduction products throughout the whole CO2R process with
only a trivial amount of CH4 produced (Figure 3c). While the FE of CO reached its utmost (28.9 ± 1.4%) at −0.8 VRHE, C2H4 appeared at −1.0 VRHE and rose incrementally to 26.6 ± 4.6% at −1.7 VRHE. The current density of C2H4 increased to 3.6 ± 0.6 mA cm−2 at −1.9 VRHE, whereas that of CH4 was less than 0.2 mA cm−2 within the entire potential range (Figure S11). Note that the Faradaic efficiencies and current densities observed in this study are at the lower bound when compared to some of the literature values,19,23 which again can be attributed to the aforementioned material and instrumental restrictions when testing copper foils in H-cell. To further verify that this is not due to the limitation of CO2 mass transport, we tested the catalytic behavior of Cu(111)-HO in higher electrolyte concentration and CO2 flow rate and observed a similar trend of FEs except for a slightly higher overall current density (Figure S12). Taken together, in comparison among the above three Cu(111) foils with different oxidation levels, we can clearly see that the overall CO2R performance, especially the C2H4 yield, increases with increasing oxidation degree. Under the highly reductive electrolytic conditions of CO2R, the reduction of the copper oxides is unavoidable, and thus it is important to trace the dynamics of the product evolution for evaluating the catalytic stability of the oxidized Cu(111) foils. Figure 3d shows that during the 200 min testing period at an applied potential of −1.6 VRHE, the FE of H2 from HER on Cu(111)-LO rose quickly from 41.9% to 95.0%, and meanwhile, all the CO2R products diminished to small FE values less than 3%. Of note, when switching the Pt counter electrode to a carbon rod electrode, the FE of H2 production during the 200 min test was mostly unchanged (Figure S13), indicating that with the current two-compartment H-cell setup the use of Pt counter electrode does not augment the HER reaction on the working electrode side. A similar trend was also observed for Cu(111)-MO, but the full deactivation of the catalyst foil took a longer time, until ∼400 min (Figure 3e). For Cu(111)-HO, the FE of C2H4 production can last stably for about 200 min, followed by a gradual decay to 4.7% at the 400th min (Figure 3f). It is worth noting that on both Cu(111)-MO and Cu(111)-HO the highest CO2R performance was typically obtained after 15−30 min starting from the beginning of the electrolytic process, indicating that a prereduction is necessary for the oxidized Cu samples to achieve the optimal activities. In general, the ultimate deactivation of all the oxidized Cu(111) catalysts seems to correlate well with their complete reduction after prolonged testing, which will be further elucidated below via postelectrolytic and operando characterizations. SEM images of all the postelectrolytic Cu(111) foils (hereafter abbreviated as post-Cu(111)-LO, post-Cu(111)MO, post-Cu(111)-HO, respectively) after the stability tests show a fragmented morphology, with the degree of fragmentation escalating with the increased Cu oxidation (Figure S14). Particularly, on the post-Cu(111)-HO surface one can clearly see the initially agglomerated CuOx clusters (Figure 2c) disintegrate into numerous finer particles (Figure S14c). Both XRD and Raman spectra taken from all postelectrolytic samples revealed no signatures belonging to any form of copper oxides (Figure S15a,b). Furthermore, the XPS Cu 2p spectra (Figure S15c) are unable to distinguish any Cu2+ species and Cu+ satellites. These observations strongly attest that after the prolonged stability test, the oxide particles
https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpclett.1c00588 J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 2021, 12, 3941−3950
3945
initially formed on Cu(111) were fragmented and fully reduced, coinciding with the loss of CO2R activity. As such, one can reasonably presume that there must exist a
transition state between the initial oxide phase and the ultimate Cu0 phase accounting for the enhanced CO2R activity. As aforementioned, on Cu(111)-HO the highest C2H4 FE was typically observed after 30 min starting from the electrolytic process. We then specially examined the Cu(111)-HO electrode taken out from the electrolyzer after 40 min of CO2R at −1.6 VRHE (referred to as post-Cu(111)-HO (40 min)) using SEM, XRD, XPS, and AES. The SEM image in Figure 4a shows that the oxide particles initially formed on Cu(111)-HO are partially disintegrated but not yet fully broken into fragmented species as seen in Figure S14c. Although both XRD (Figure S16) and XPS (Figure S17) were unable to detect any oxide species and positive Cu states, respectively, the AES Cu LMM spectrum clearly shows the coexistence of Cu+ and Cu0 species (Figure S18). By contrast, the AES spectrum of post-Cu(111)-HO (7 h) only exhibits a singlet Cu0 peak (Figure S19). Therefore, both the SEM morphology and AEM Cu state of post-Cu(111)-HO (40 min) indicate that it was only partially reduced, whereas the sample
of post-Cu(111)-HO (7 h) represents a more reduced state of OD-Cu. Since Raman, as shown in Figure 2e, is very sensitive to detect the oxidized form of Cu, operando Raman spectroscopy was then performed to monitor the evolution of CuOx on Cu(111)-HO during CO2R. As shown in Figure 4b, after 1000 s of electrolysis, the characteristic Raman peaks of CuO at 298 and 632 cm−1 mostly disappeared while those of Cu2O below 220 cm−1 dropped their intensity. After 2000 s, even the Cu2O peaks were nearly gone, indicative of mostly reduced Cu surface. By the time of 3000 s and thereafter, there was no Raman response at all between 100 and 900 cm−1, suggesting the residual and subsurface oxides left, if there are any, are under the detection limit. Collectively, both the ex situ AES and in situ Raman studies indicate that the copper oxide surface is gradually reduced during CO2R, and it takes a longer time to fully reduce a more oxidized surface. By measuring the electrochemically active surface area (EASA), we further compared the roughness factors of Cu(111)-LO, Cu(111)-MO, and Cu(111)-HO and monitored their evolution along the CO2R process. First, we found the EASA values of all three samples before the CO2R test are very small and insignificant for a meaningful comparison. Second,
https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpclett.1c00588 J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 2021, 12, 3941−3950
3946
the EASA of the OD-Cu surfaces kept changing during CO2R. When comparing the post-Cu(111)-HO samples at 0 min, 40 min, and 7 h (Figure S20), we observed an obvious increase of EASA with time. This is in accordance with previous SEM observations showing more fragmented surface morphology with extended time. However, despite the increase in EASA, the CO2R activity of post-Cu(111)-HO (7 h) is worse than that of post-Cu(111)-HO (40 min), suggesting that in our case the surface roughness factor does not correlate to the catalytic activity. Besides, the gradually changed EASA with time might also help support that the copper oxide surface is gradually reduced during CO2R. Lastly, when comparing the samples of post-Cu(111)-LO (40 min), Cu(111)-MO (40 min), and Cu(111)-HO (40 min), we observed that the EASA values increased with the increasing oxidation degree (Figure S21), indicating that the overall roughness of OD-Cu correlates to the degree of Cu(111) oxidation. To further interrogate the polycrystallinity and stochastic facet exposure of the reduced and fragmented CuOx layer on the Cu(111)-HO foils, we utilized focus ion beam (FIB) to cut out thin cross sections from the post-Cu(111)-HO (40 min) and post-Cu(111)-HO (7 h) and analyzed them using transmission Kikuchi diffraction (TKD)54 and HR-TEM. TKD mappings in Figure 4c and Figure 4d show both the post-Cu(111)-HO (40 min) and post-Cu(111)-HO (7 h) samples own rich and diversely orientated facets at the subsurface of the OD-Cu, accompanied by extensive grain boundaries due to the fragmentation of the oxide particles (the black background is due to the fact that the crystal grains are too small for facet identification by the TKD method). The polycrystallinity of these OD-Cu samples with extensive grain boundaries and multiple facet-exposure is further corroborated by the atomic images and SAED patterns (Figure 4e,f) from HR-TEM, as well as the AFM topographic images (Figure S22). Nonetheless, despite the similar grain features, postCu(111)-HO (40 min) exhibited fairly good CO2R activity, whereas post-Cu(111)-HO (7 h) was barely CO2R-active. Collectively from the above spectroscopic, microscopic, and electrochemical investigations, it becomes clear that either the polycrystallinity or the grain boundaries of OD-Cu do not impart prominent CO2R activities. Instead, it should be the transition state between the initial oxide phase and the finally reduced copper playing a more critical role to account for the observed CO2R activity. This is experimentally analogous to the simulation results by Xiao et al. attributing the mixed Cu+/ Cu0 state to synergically improving both CO2 activation and CO dimerization.38
In summary, single crystal Cu(111) foils were successfully prepared and employed to study the catalytic CO2R behavior by minimizing convolutions from the initial surface heterogeneity and polycrystallinity, which have been typically neglected by previous studies. We found that in their pristine states, both the thermally annealed p-Cu and Cu(111) foils exhibited major HER activities and very limited CO2R performance. By exposure of the two samples to ambient air for just 1 day, a slight surface oxidation would significantly promote both the CO2R activity and kinetics. Next, by deliberately oxidizing the Cu(111) foils to various degrees, we found the overall CO2R performance, especially the C2H4 selectivity, correlated linearly with the oxidation level. Postelectrolytic and operando characterizations revealed that the CuOx particles initially formed on the oxidized foils were gradually reduced and fragmented, but either the polycrys-
tallinity or grain boundaries of the OD-Cu are not the essential cause of the activity enhancement. Instead, a transition state between the initial oxide phase and the final reduced copper dictates the catalytic property of OD-Cu in CO2R. By employment of the single crystal Cu(111) surface, our study here furnishes a better understanding of the CO2R process catalyzed by OD-Cu and suggests that a long-last transition state between the oxidized and fully reduced states should be in favor of the CO2R stability.
